messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Vignette:
Leilani had always found a certain comfort in the logic of the night. As a cybersecurity analyst, her best work was often done after hours, in the quiet hum of servers, untangling complex threats in lines of code. That all changed six months ago. Driving home from the office on a rain-slicked road, the sudden glare of headlights swerving into her lane was the last thing she saw clearly. The world became a chaotic series of snapshots: the spiderweb of cracks erupting across her windshield, the violent jolt as her body was thrown against the seatbelt, the acrid, chemical smell of the deployed airbag. The other car never stopped. The sharp, crushing pain in her collarbone and ribs was immediate, but the lingering injustice of the hit-and-run would prove to be a wound of a different kind.

In the weeks that followed, as her physical injuries began to mend, Leilani found her mind had become a treacherous place. The memory of the accident was not a coherent story but a collection of intrusive, still images. While reviewing a security log at her desk, the image of the shattered glass would flash behind her eyes, brilliant and terrifying. The pain was the most bewildering part; a sudden, sharp ache would bloom in her shoulder, an exact echo of the impact, so real she would gasp and clutch at her chest. Sometimes, with no warning, a phantom scent of gasoline and burnt plastic would fill her nostrils, bringing with it a wave of nausea and primal fear. She began a desperate, silent campaign to scrub these fragments from her mind, burying herself in the most complex encryption problems she could find, hoping to overwrite the data of that night with the clean logic of her work.

Her home, once a sanctuary, now felt like an unsecured network after dark. Night was no longer a time of quiet focus but of heightened threat. Leilani found it impossible to simply fall asleep; she had to remain alert, listening to every creak of the house, every car that passed on the street. Sleep, when it came, was shallow and brittle. She would often jolt awake in the pitch black, her heart hammering, seized by an urgent need to check the locks on the doors and windows, peering through the blinds to ensure no one was out there. The feeling of safety had become a temporary state she had to actively re-establish, night after night.

A profound sense of distrust had settled deep within her. She had come to believe her body was a traitor, an unreliable vessel that had failed her once and was destined to do so again. Every normal ache sent a ripple of panic through her. But the feeling of betrayal was sharpest when she thought of the driver who had simply sped away. The question of *why* it happened to her, and why there was no accountability, became a circular, unanswerable argument she had with herself for hours on end. It felt, she explained, deeply and fundamentally unfair. This sense of being wronged manifested as a strange kind of shame. When she was in the office, she felt exposed, certain that her colleagues could see the trauma on her, as if it were a visible scar on her face. To manage this, she began to retreat, keeping interactions brief and avoiding the break room. She started declining invitations from friends and family, finding the effort of feeling anything—joy, sadness, even simple connection—to be utterly exhausting. It was easier to feel nothing at all.

Leilani finally sought help after a performance review where her manager, with genuine concern, noted her increasing isolation and distraction. The feedback felt like another system failure, this time a professional one. She sat in the therapist’s office, a woman accustomed to control now feeling completely powerless. Her greatest fear was that this state of constant, vigilant alert was permanent. Her greatest hope was simply to one day feel safe in the dark again, to trust her own body, and to sleep through the night without having to wake up and check if the world was secure.
